en: (1) Then, having ascertained that the site is free from all defects of misfortune, one should sow barley in the center of that plot of land; thereafter, one should let the cows graze there upon the green grass. Then, on the purified ground—which is of a peaceful nature and sprinkled with milk mixed with their urine and dung—one should observe the entire procedure, beginning with the [propitiation of] the *nāgas*.
(2) Following that:

Those who desire to construct monasteries, shrines, hermitages, palaces, towers, temples, and so forth, must examine the "site-nāga" (vāstunāga) here; that portion of ground which is square is [the site].
In each of the directions, the division of the earth occurs here over three months by means of the number of days;
having divided the ninety-fold portion of the eastern land situated between the northeast and the southeast.
In the intermediate space between the directions of Agni and Nairṛti, and likewise from the direction of Nairṛti to Vāyu;
and at the boundary of the direction of Vāyu and the Lord of Beings (Bhūtādhipati), one should likewise make a division of ninety [parts].
(3) From the months of Bhādra, Āśvina, and Kārttika, its head is directed toward the northeast,
its tail-towards the southwest, and its secret organ is placed in the center of the earth.
Below the navel, his body is that of a serpent; above it, he has a human form endowed with a hood.
Facing south, he holds a jewel at his ear with his left hand, and his other hand rests upon his hip.
Covering nine divisions of the earth, the Naga indeed lies there, situated at the base of the world-pillar;
his body-staff extends to the eastern and western limits of the quarters, reaching as far as the measured circle of the earth's regions.
By means of the single movement of the sun, there is a division of one day and night at the beginning of each successive day;
according to the logic [of this], the movement through the divisions occurs likewise in the eastern, western, and northern directions.
Beginning from the white fortnight (the bright half of the month), during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha, his face and gaze are directed toward the western quarter,
his head is turned toward the southeastern quarter, and his lower body is situated in the northwestern corner.
In the month of Phālguna, during the month of Madhu (Caitra), his face is directed toward the quarter of the Lord of Yakṣas (the East),
his head is turned toward the direction of the South-West corner, and the part of his tail is in the direction of the North-East corner.
In the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, and Śrāvaṇa, its face is turned toward the eastern direction,
its head is directed toward the northwestern corner, and its tail portion faces the southeastern quarter.
In a single year, he traversed the earth in every direction, not merely by way of a few good roads;
for he had specifically learned, month after month, the various shifts in the movements of the lord of serpents.

Having visualized the beautiful Vairocana, whose nature consists of the remainder of white light, one should worship the eight lords of the *nāgas* upon his body, beginning from the tail, with milk and various offerings.
At the upper part of the penis is Kulika, deep blue; at the secret organ is Karkoṭaka, resembling a dark hue;
at the navel is Śaṅkhapāla, like a lotus stalk; and on the arm is Mahāpadma, with the luster of gold.
Vāsuki, resembling dūrvā grass, is situated in the heart; the one named Takṣaka, red in color, is located in the throat;
Padma, radiant with white rays, is in the ear; and the blue serpent Ananta is situated on the head.
(5) Having meditated upon himself as the manifestation of Vighnāntaka, firm and holding a spade marked with a vajra,
he first pacifies the army of Māra by means of that raised left hand.
While scattering the fourfold oblation toward the directions presided over by Indra, the Lord of Wealth, and the others,
one should cast the clay from that site— placed at the offering spot— with the *Śānti-hṛdaya* mantra, outside the corners beginning with the southeast.
Then, with a well-disposed mind, one should diligently scatter that fifth layer of earth in the center of the site;
and that fifth layer, being excavated by many laborers in the cardinal and intermediate directions, [should be prepared].
(6) Having left aside the ground consisting of the final twenty-one divisions, one should bury [the pillar] in the other nine divisions according to its shape.
That ground situated in front of the central "lap" division brings about auspiciousness and bestows the successful attainment of the increase of the qualities of dharma, artha, and kāma.

If death should occur for one's mother, father, daughter, son, siblings, wife, daughter-in-law, kinsmen, relatives, or friends, then one should indeed dig into the earth at the square situated in the ninth division. This is the place of the serpent.

If [the omen] falls on the back, there will be either self-destruction, displacement from one's position, or the loss of considerable wealth; if it falls on the tail, there will be the destruction of elephants, horses, buffaloes, goats, cattle, and other animals, as well as the loss of followers, servants, and strength.
If wood should prevail among the five [substances] that cause malice, there will be danger from anthills; if from hair, nails, or ashes, minor ailments;
if from stone, fear of wind; if from husks or burnt wood, various fevers; and if from bones, the disease of colic.
Having understood the various signs of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, the preceptor, the artisans, and the patron must perform their duties;
having quickly cleared the entire surface of the ground of all debris, they should fill the excavation completely on all sides with pure earth.

Therefore, those who determine that the serpent (*vāstunāga*) lies upon the central Brahma-thread (*madhyabrahmasūtra*) act out of ignorance and cause harm to the teaching. Many authorities maintain that the serpent’s sleep proceeds from the northeast corner, extending through the cardinal directions in the sequence of days during three-month periods beginning with Bhādrapada. Thus concludes the procedure for examining the serpent of the site (*vāstunāga*).
